title: Arrays and Spans: Many Readings at Once

questions.question: What happens when you read readings[5] from an array of five doubles?
options: It reads whatever bytes follow the array, with no error reported
The program stops with an index out of range error
It returns zero
It wraps around and returns readings[0]
questions.explanation: C++ does not check array bounds. Reading past the end is undefined behaviour and often returns a plausible looking wrong value.

questions.question: What is a span made of?
options: A pointer to the first element and a count, with no ownership
A copy of the data it was created from
A growable buffer like a vector
A reference counted handle to shared memory
questions.explanation: A span is a view. It owns nothing, copies nothing, and becomes dangerous the moment the data it points at goes away.

questions.question: Why does median copy the samples before sorting?
options: The span is a read only view, so sorting it would reorder the caller's data
Because std::sort cannot work on doubles
To make the function faster
Because spans cannot be iterated
questions.explanation: A function taking a read only view must not have side effects on the caller's array. Copying into a vector keeps the promise the signature makes.

questions.question: Five readings are 1.00, 1.02, 0.98, 1.01 and 4.70. Which filter handles the spike better?
options: The median, because one wild value does not move the middle
The mean, because it uses all the data
Both handle it equally
Neither, a spike always corrupts the output
questions.explanation: The mean is dragged upward by the outlier. The median only cares about ordering, so a single spike leaves the middle value untouched.

questions.question: Why does the moving average use a shorter window at the start of the stream?
options: There is no data before the first reading, and padding with zeros would bias the output
To make the output vector shorter
Because the window must always be odd
To avoid dividing by zero
questions.explanation: Averaging over what actually exists is honest. Padding with zeros would pull the first few outputs towards zero for no physical reason.

questions.question: What is the danger of returning a span from a function?
options: It may point at data that was destroyed when the function returned
Spans cannot be returned at all
The caller receives a copy, which defeats the purpose
It forces the caller to sort the data
questions.explanation: A span does not keep its data alive. Returning one that views a local vector leaves the caller with a view of destroyed memory.
